articles.title: United Airlines CEO: 'We should have a national wealth tax'
articles.summary: United CEO Scotty Kirby says wealth inequality is 'a danger to our society.'
articles.body:
United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby gave a wide-ranging, often provocative interview to the New York Times, defending fees for aisle and window seats and countering the rise in airfares by asserting "it's expensive to fly airplanes."

"There are customers that pay more that get more," Kirby, 59, said in the interview that ran Oct. 18 .

But he struck a decidedly more populist note on the topic of wealth inequality — which he brought up when the Times asked him about waning trust in CEOs and his responsibility in dispelling it. Here's his full answer:

"Wealth inequality has become a danger to our society, and we need to address that," he said. "We should have a national wealth tax — it won't work by state because people will just move. And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them."

United Airlines stock rose 0.3% before the bell on Tuesday.

Kirby is not the first or only business titan to call for bigger taxes on the wealthiest Americans. Luminaries like Warren Buffett, Bill Gates, and George Soros have long advocated for increasing the tax burden at their rarefied wealth levels.

"We've updated our tax system before to keep up with changing times, and we need to do it again, starting with raising taxes on people like me," Gates wrote on his blog in 2020.

Marc Benioff, CEO of Salesforce ( CRM ), wrote in 2019 that "increasing taxes on high-income individuals like myself would help generate the trillions of dollars that we desperately need to improve education and healthcare and fight climate change."

Joe Biden was president, and Democrats in Congress were gearing up to pass legislation to tax unrealized gains on individuals with a net worth of at least $1 billion or annual income of $100 million for three consecutive years. Of course, that never happened, and after President Trump was reelected, Republicans in Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included provisions that made lower marginal tax rates for high incomes permanent, along with other provisions benefiting wealthy Americans.

As for the inheritance taxes Kirby said he favors, there is no federal tax on individual beneficiaries of inherited assets. A few states impose a state inheritance tax.

There is a federal estate tax, but the exemption is so large — $15 million per person — that few people ever pay it. Only 0.2% of estates are large enough to be subject to the tax, and even then the tax applies only to the amount that exceeds the exemption threshold.

Molly Moorhead is economics editor for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title: Beyond the Strait: Gulf looks for an escape route from Hormuz
articles.summary: The Middle East conflict has put the world’s energy lifeline, the Strait of Hormuz, in a chokehold. But the Gulf might be looking for an escape route.
articles.body: The Middle East conflict has put the world’s energy lifeline, the Strait of Hormuz, in a chokehold.But the Gulf might be looking for an escape route.Over the next five years, countries in the region could invest in alternative logistics corridors and energy pipelines to loosen their dependence on the strategic waterway and keep oil and gas flowing, HSBC group chief executive Georges Elhedery said on Tuesday.The conflict has exposed the risks of depending on the strategic waterway, which previously carried a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade. Gulf nations are now being pushed to direct resources towards developing energy pipelines connecting production centres to ports, potentially allowing shipments to bypass the strait.Speaking at the HSBC Future Forum in Dubai, Elhedery said the region would be able to recover from the conflict and continue growing, but that doing so would require substantial investment."We do see this region being able to recover and then continue growing. It will mean a lot of investment," the bank CEO said."Of course, we do wish and hope to see a resolution to the conflict ... But Hormuz, probably in five years' time, may become redundant," he added.$1.4 trillion infrastructure pipelineThe shift towards alternative routes comes as the Middle East, North Africa and Turkey have a substantial pipeline of infrastructure projects that could attract investment.According to an HSBC report published on Monday, citing data from Dubai-based construction industry market intelligence platform MEED, the regions are offering $872 billion in individual project packages. These form part of a wider $1.4 trillion pipeline of infrastructure projects that have been planned but not yet awarded.The investment pipeline comes as Gulf countries consider ways to limit the disruption caused by the conflict and strengthen their ability to move energy supplies through routes other than the Strait of Hormuz.Gulf remains attractive to investors despite warDespite the conflict, business leaders and institutional investors continue to view the Gulf as an attractive destination for investment.A recent HSBC survey of more than 1,600 business leaders and around 820 global institutional investors found that respondents still considered the region an appealing investment hub.However, the economic outlook for the wider region has weakened. After recording growth of 3.3% in 2025, the Middle East, North Africa and Pakistan region is expected to contract by 1.3% this year because of the war, according to a World Bank forecast issued last week.The contraction is expected to be followed by a strong but uneven recovery in 2027.Elhedery was among the global financiers expected to attend Saudi Arabia's flagship investment conference next week. The event was postponed until 2027 on Monday following deadly strikes in Riyadh by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: France’s crisis sounds familiar. Is America next?
articles.summary: France is on fire, and it faces a political and an economic reckoning that feels dangerously familiar to Americans.
articles.body: France is on fire, and it faces a political and an economic reckoning that feels dangerously familiar to Americans. The country is nearing a fiscal crisis, because it spent more than it can afford to pay back. The bill is coming due much faster than expected after bond rates surged in recent months, boosted by rising energy costs. Raising taxes and reducing government spending are part of a potential solution, but those would be politically unpopular decisions that could risk further angering an already livid public. Any workable solution faces a steep climb in an uncertain budget battle in a sharply divided government. Does that ring a bell? A growing number of countries are facing struggles similar to France’s — in particular, the United Kingdom — where rapidly growing debt, surging costs to finance that borrowing and insufficient political will to make the uncomfortable decisions to solve the problem are the story of Western economics right now. That includes the United States. But similarities can be superficial. France’s financial stress is particularly acute. The risk of contagion throughout Europe is low. France’s enormous public safety net represents a much larger share of government spending than that in the United States. And the unique dynamics of the American economy means the United States faces no imminent danger of becoming the next France. The problem These are not new problems: Europe’s social safety net has been on an unsustainable path for decades, and economists and some politicians have warned for years that the bill would eventually come due. But they’re getting worse. The Iran war exacerbated the West’s fiscal problems. Since February, the G7 economies’ average 10-year government bond yield grew more than 1 percentage point, reaching the highest level in nearly 20 years, the International Monetary Fund reported last week. By the end of the decade, those seven economies’ public debt loads are expected to collectively exceed their economic production, the IMF predicts. That would be the first time since World War II. France’s public debt is around 119% of its GDP, double the European Union’s target, and its annual budget deficit is 5.4% of its gross domestic product. “In Europe, people are increasingly scared of the bond market and the interest rates that governments need to pay to borrow,” said Peter Taylor-Gooby, a social policy professor at the University of Kent. “It’s come to a point where you can’t ignore it anymore. If we do, we’ll reach a serious crisis.” On paper, America doesn’t look dissimilar: Its $32 trillion public debt is roughly equal to annual US GDP, and the $2 trillion budget deficit that it just closed the books on is more than 6% of GDP. The cost to finance America’s public debt just crossed $1 trillion a year, an astounding 14% of the total federal budget. In other words, one in every seven tax dollars is used just to pay interest on the amount of money the United States is borrowing. But the serious conversations about cutting back on spending and raising taxes taking place in Europe are considerably less serious in the United States. So why isn’t the United States facing the same problems as France? Why it won’t happen in the US…yet The United States’ biggest advantage is that it prints the world’s reserve currency. The majority of global transactions are conducted in US dollars, including key commodities like oil and gold. Demand for dollars remains robust in large part because they’re considered safe: The United States’ transparency and commitment to the rule of law make the dollar the cornerstone of the global financial system — even if some of the shine has worn off over the past decade. That also fuels demand for US Treasuries, widely considered the safest of safe-haven assets. Even in the midst of a global government bond sell-off, US bond rates remain lower than those of other Western economies. And when stocks went on a skid last week, investors were unafraid to turn to their traditional place of refuge, sending Treasury yields sharply lower in the process. But the difference between France and the United States really comes down to one thing. As James Carville said: It’s the economy, stupid. The United States also has a uniquely large and diverse economy that is far less susceptible to shocks than many of its smaller peers. AI in particular is producing an investment boom in the United States that is lifting the economy when several other sectors appear to be stagnating or in decline. One key way to make deficits less relevant is to keep the economy growing strong. That makes the debt look puny by comparison. So countries need to ask: What is the rate we’re paying — and is it sustainable for us to keep paying it based on our expected economic growth?” “France and the UK are pretty close,” noted Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics. “But in the US, AI’s contributions to growth make it more likely we’ll manage our debts and navigate it much more gracefully.” Economists warn: Don’t confuse the lack of a looming debt crisis in the United States with fiscal responsibility. It’s just that it can handle the problem better than France or the UK. “That doesn’t mean we should take any solace in that,” added Zandi. “We’re just in a different place.” Could it happen elsewhere? Any time a European country faces a fiscal problem, it raises concerns about a contagion that could spread across the continent. But economists widely view France’s problems as contained within the country. The European Central Bank has signaled it would not need to intervene in France’s fiscal situation. But it could if it had to, and it is well-positioned to buy up a bunch of bonds of its member countries to limit any potential contagion effects, noted Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics. Other European economies’ deficits are also much smaller by comparison. Some are expected to run surpluses this year. And French political parties across the left and right have said they want to remain with the European Union — including French presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen, a far-right candidate who once championed “Frexit” but has since backed off that pledge. Although Germany’s AfD party has advocated leaving the EU, it isn’t close to forming a government yet, Kenningham noted. But an X factor could lead to a debt crisis outside France: the US “X date.” At some point next year, the United States will hit its debt ceiling again, and the new Congress will need to negotiate with President Donald Trump to raise it — a political football that could be particularly challenged by a lame duck president and a potentially Democratic-controlled Congress less willing to give in. A failure to raise the debt ceiling threatens to force the United States to manufacture a default on its debt, even if it otherwise would be able to pay. “You could construct a scenario in which we breach the debt limit by Halloween next year,” said Zandi. “And then you’ve got other issues.”

articles.title: Millionaire renters are growing. Why they're choosing to rent vs buy
articles.summary: The number of millionaire renters is surging as affluent Americans increasingly choose mobility over homeownership.
articles.body:
Millionaire renters are on the rise, growing at a faster pace than millionaire homeowners, according to a report from RentCafe .

Between 2020 and 2024, the number of millionaire renter households remained small compared to homeowners, but it was growing at a much faster pace, the apartment search platform found after analyzing American Community Survey estimates. Millionaire renters grew 229%, or more than tripled in just five years. That's faster than the 193% jump in millionaire homeowners over the same period.

Preferring to rent marks a shift in housing preferences as affluent Americans have long favored owning, which has been a hallmark of the 'American Dream.'

"For a growing number of millionaires, renting is now a deliberate choice," the report said. "That's because many prioritize mobility without the commitment of owning a home, as well as the ability to relocate without going through the lengthy process of selling a multi-million-dollar house."

Also, "rather than tying up capital in real estate, many affluent renters prefer to keep their money liquid and invest in a stock market that's posted strong gains," it said.

Millionaire renters are usually millionaire households due to double high incomes (75%), the report said. Only a quarter are individual millionaires.

They also tend to be younger. Nearly half of millionaire renters (49%) are Millennials, but Gen Z has posted the fastest surge in millionaire renters, the report said. The number of Gen Z millionaire renters increased 46-fold to more than 400 households in 2024 from fewer than a dozen in 2020, it said. However, Gen Z makes up only 2% of all millionaire renters, RentCafe noted.

"This generation was barely entering the workforce in 2020," said Adina Dragos, RentCafe writer and research analyst. "By 2024, the oldest Gen Zers were approaching 30, and many who struck it big early — through the creator economy, crypto or startup equity — were choosing to rent precisely because their wealth isn't tied to a traditional career ladder. With no employer anchoring them to one place, they have little reason to put down roots."

What do millionaire renters do for a living?

Most of these folks are in white-collar, high-earning fields, like chief executives, tech professionals and top financial managers that don't necessarily require them to work in one specific location, RentCafe said.

However, there were some surprises like high-earning professors and operations managers, "a sign that the millionaire renter isn't always who you'd expect," it said.

articles.title: Nscale, Anthropic in Talks for $45 Billion Cloud Computing Deal
articles.summary: Nscale Ltd., the AI cloud computing firm, is in talks to sell computing power to Anthropic PBC in a deal that could be worth about $45 billion, according to...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Nscale Ltd., the AI cloud computing firm, is in talks to sell computing power to Anthropic PBC ( ANTH.PVT ) in a deal that could be worth about $45 billion, according to people familiar with the negotiations.

The Nvidia Corp.-backed data center developer is seeking a second major deal with the firm behind Claude for a second facility at its Monarch data center campus in West Virginia, the people said. Anthropic has agreements in place with Nscale for infrastructure that's worth as much as about $44.6 billion, according to a regulatory filing for Nscale's planned initial public offering.

The second Monarch building would deliver 460 megawatts of computing power, using Nvidia's advanced Vera Rubin AI chips, some of the people said. Anthropic also has the right of first refusal on Monarch's expected third building, they said.

A deal could be finalized as soon as in the coming days, the people said, asking not to be identified as the discussions are private. Deliberations are ongoing, details of the plan could change and no final decisions have been made, the people said. Representatives for Anthropic and Nscale declined to comment.

Another multibillion-dollar computing deal would bolster Nscale's IPO prospects as it seeks about a $30 billion valuation in its market debut. A cohort of investors urged the firm to lower its IPO valuation target, Bloomberg News has reported.

Anthropic, which is one of Nscale's biggest customers, has emerged as a major client for data center providers in general. Deals it has inked include a $50 billion pact with Fluidstack Ltd., $10 billion with infrastructure startup Volta Infrastructure Holdings Ltd. and $45 billion with Elon Musk's SpaceX.

Nscale's Monarch campus in West Virginia is scalable to more than 8 gigawatts of gross power when complete, the IPO filing documents show.

Part of the Monarch campus was initially expected to be leased by Microsoft Corp., which had announced in March it signed a letter of intent for the planned data center. But Microsoft walked away from the West Virginia site in the summer, allowing Anthropic to become the tenant, Bloomberg News reported.

Anthropic, which was valued at $965 billion in May, is expected to conduct its own potentially record-breaking IPO in the coming months, and continues to hunt for more computing power to keep growing.

articles.title: Homebuilders haven't felt this bad about the market since 2012
articles.summary: Homebuilder confidence has cratered as rising rates and high inflation dampens sales.
articles.body:
Homebuilder confidence slumped to the lowest level since 2012 as builders contend with rising mortgage rates, high materials costs, and a challenging labor market.

Confidence in the market for new single-family homes fell three points to 29 in October, according to the latest National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index reading. The last time the reading was this low, the housing market was slowly working its way back from the depths of the financial crisis.

Mortgage rates above 7% , high gas prices , and elevated inflation have all sapped buyer interest in new construction homes. In response, 43% of builders cut prices in October, the highest share so far this decade. And 65% are using sales incentives, such as mortgage rate buydowns, to attract buyers.

Making matters worse, the cost of construction loans, diesel, and construction materials are all on the rise. Immigration enforcement is also weighing on builders' ability to find and keep workers.

Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

articles.title: 1.6 million pounds of hot dogs recalled amid USDA staffing cuts — and investors are feeling the impact
articles.summary: A wave of food recalls is rattling consumers and investors. Here's how stock prices respond.
articles.body:
If you're sitting down in your work or school lunch room, looking at your plate and wondering — "Can I safely eat this?" — you're not the only one.

This year has brought a seemingly non-stop parade of scary-sounding, wide-reaching food recalls, starting with the so-called "diarrhea lettuce" over the summer. That turned out to be an outbreak of a parasite called cyclospora, which had contaminated lettuce distributed by Taylor Farms and served at restaurants and grocery stores in dozens of states.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

Then came the Star Meat Delivery affair: According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture ( USDA ), the Lucama, North Carolina-based company put false labels on 167,639 pounds of raw pork, beef, and goat products, implying that they had been inspected when they hadn't been. No illness has been linked to the meat, but all of it had to be recalled.

And now, nearly 1.6 million pounds of processed, ready-to-eat meat products such as hot dogs and deli meat made by Kayem Foods are being recalled because they may not have been stored at safe temperatures. No reports of illness have emerged, but you can see if anything in your fridge is affected here .

Everyone understands the human cost of these events — in the case of the cyclospora outbreak alone, 20,000 people became ill and two died. But what about the business consequences? Can a company that becomes known for diarrhea lettuce or potentially tainted meat ever bounce back?

It's too early to say if the number of food recalls or outbreaks have increased this year, or why. However, experts have raised concerns about the loss of federal capacity to study and monitor food safety due to sweeping cuts at the USDA, the Food and Drug Administration, and other agencies.

According to Investigate Midwest , between January and June of 2025, the USDA reduced its workforce by 18%, and the Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), which is responsible for inspecting slaughterhouses and processing plants, cut staff by 9%. According to a May 2026 USDA report , consumer complaints about the safety of meat, poultry and egg products jumped nearly 40% last year.

articles.title: In Europe, budget airlines thrive. Why not the US?
articles.summary: The low-cost carrier business model dominates short-haul flying in Europe. But ‘budget’ airlines have struggled to take hold in the United States.
articles.body: At the top of one of Ryanair’s European website’s reads “fly “FROM 24.99€.” The Irish-based airline is one of the most profitable low-cost carriers in the world with a network that crisscrosses Europe. The success lies in its commitment to its business model, which cuts airline costs to the bone while charging passengers for everything. Travelers pay for baggage, seat reservations, in-person check-in or using a credit card. Ryanair even floated the idea of charging to use the bathroom or getting rid of seats and having passengers stand, though neither took flight. The low-cost carrier business model dominates short-haul flying in Europe, which analysts say account for over 40% of available seats. Many passengers have come to accept no frills flying, paying for every extra beyond a seat. Last year, Ryanair flew more than 200 million passengers. English low-cost carrier easyJet flew nearly 100 million passengers, Hungary’s Wizz Air nearly 70 million, and Spanish airline Vueling carried 38 million. That same business model, however, has struggled to take hold in the United States. The largest US budget airline, Frontier, only flew 33 million passengers during the same time frame. Part of that is cultural — Americans have a lower tolerance for bare-bones service and don’t love paying extra for flight add-ons. But there are geographic reasons, like shorter distances for flights, as well as economic ones, like inflationary pressures and rising airfares. Low-cost carriers are run differently in Europe Ryanair has a strong balance sheet, reporting passenger growth each quarter over the last year. But that success took “30 years of decision-making, where operational cost is the No. 1 driver,” according to Mike Arnot, an airline industry consultant. The low-cost carrier model, he said, is built around removing as much expense as possible from an airline operation, like flying a single type of aircraft, minimizing maintenance costs or using stairs instead of jet bridges to save on airport fees. Garth Lund, who worked in leadership at low-cost airline group Wizz Air for nearly eight years, said European budget carriers are “unwavering in their commitment to low costs.” “They have really stuck to the original business model and not allowed themselves to get distracted, and as a result, they’ve maintained their cost structure better than the US airlines have,” Lund said. One example, he said, is that the European airlines design schedules so that crews don’t spend nights in cities away from home, saving hotel costs. He also points to the hours that airline crews can work. In Europe, there are fewer unions limiting shifts. “That efficiency has a big knock-on effect on the cost structure,” Lund said. European airports are different Some airports in Europe have been designed to keep the budget carriers moving quickly and affordably. “In Europe, airports nowadays are really designed for low-cost airlines,” Lund said. Compare turn times, for example, or how long it takes to deplane passengers, service an aircraft and load it for the next departure. The longer it takes, the fewer flights an aircraft can fly in one day and less money the airline earns. US airports can sometimes log 45 minutes to one hour. Many European airports are down to 25 to 30 minutes, he said. That’s because boarding in Europe can happen in the front and back of the aircraft, depending on the airport, and don’t always use jet bridges like most American carriers do. In Europe, there are also many secondary airports in large cities. This makes it easier, and cheaper, to open new routes. For example, Munich International Airport is a major hub for Germany, but a low-cost alternative is a little over an hour away at Memmingen Airport. Wizz Air and Ryanair both fly there instead of directly to Munich. London’s Heathrow Airport also has alternatives popular with low-cost carriers, London Stansted and London Luton Airport. “In Europe, the secondary airports have become quite large airports in their own right,” Lund said. Secondary airports also exist in the US, like Dallas Love Field near DFW International Airport, or Chicago-Midway Airport, the smaller airport to Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport. However, there aren’t always multiple options like in Europe, and many of these secondary airports are dominated by carriers like Southwest. Not many low-fare airlines survive in the US American low-cost carriers have not found the same success as those in Europe. That’s partly because US consumers have trouble making the distinction between low costs and low fares, Arnot said. They assume “low-cost” refers to the price of a ticket, but it’s really about keeping operating costs low. Sometimes budget airlines do have the lowest fares. But if those low fares don’t exceed the cost base over the medium term, the airlines will fail, he said. “Not many low-fare airlines have survived, but there are good examples of low-cost airlines that have thrived,” Arnot said. “Especially at the low-cost, low-fare end of the market, the demand is highly elastic, which is a fancy marketing word for consumers can take the bus, or just not go, if the fare is not what they want to pay.” And because US discount carriers cater to those price-sensitive leisure travelers, they have a harder time raising fares. That’s difficult when increased costs squeeze their already thin margins, like rising fuel prices related to the conflict in the Middle East. Southwest and JetBlue were once the leading low-cost carriers in the US. But Southwest had a tumultuous few years following an activist investor campaign to increase profitability. JetBlue had a slow financial recovery following impacts from the pandemic. The airlines both now operate a more hybrid model between a low-cost carrier and a traditional airline. Spirit Airlines, one of the most prominent ultra-low-cost airlines in the US, collapsed earlier this year. It also had been unprofitable since the pandemic, declaring bankruptcy twice before the spike in jet fuel prices this year derailed its plan to emerge from its latest bankruptcy. Today, five low-cost carriers remain in the US — Frontier, Allegiant Air, Breeze Airways, Sun Country Airlines and Avelo Air. American legacy carriers experimented with the low-cost carrier business, with Delta Air Lines launching Song in 2003 and United creating Ted in 2004. Both carriers failed to gain traction and were shut down within several years after fuel prices spiked. But the parent airlines adopted some lessons from the ventures, like faster turnaround times. Europeans like budget carriers. American make jokes about them Europeans also don’t have a negative image associated with low-cost carriers, analysts say, while Americans often expect them to be poor quality or come with bad customer service. “In the US, I feel like there’s almost a stigma attached to flying with a low-cost airline, so Spirit was famously the butt of many jokes,” Lund said. That’s much less the case in Europe, he said, where passengers might be flying business class on British Airways one week and then not hesitate to take a coach seat on easyJet the next. The collapse of Spirit also taught American legacy airlines like Delta and United how to fend off low-cost carriers, according to Shye Gilad, former airline captain and business professor at Georgetown University. That includes matching airfare prices or offering deals, as well as introducing basic economy fares that directly compete with low-cost airlines. “They were about lowest possible fares, and of course, low frills associated with that,” Gilad said. “But I think the contrast was more stark because they’re often going head-to-head with the large legacy carriers, which do provide a pretty big contrast.”

articles.title: Walmart goes on offense to win the subscription space, offering new bundle for one price
articles.summary: Walmart is looking to win back market share after posting disappointing sales numbers last quarter.
articles.body:
As many Americans say they're strapped by subscription fatigue, Walmart is looking to make its offerings more enticing by combining Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus for $120 a year, plus tax.

The all-in-one offering announced Tuesday is only available annually, with no monthly option or trial. If you were to purchase each offer separately, Walmart+ costs $98 plus tax per year, or $12.95 plus tax per month, and its wholesale membership, Sam's Club Plus, costs $120 a year. A basic club membership runs $60.

Walmart ( WMT ) posted its slowest US same-store sales growth last quarter since Q4 of 2020, at 2.6%. Now the retailer is hoping it can recapture share it may have lost to others like Target ( TGT ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Costco ( COST ), and BJ's ( BJ ).

"We're giving people a reason to expect more from their memberships … we're raising expectations for what a membership can deliver: more money in their pockets and more time to call their own," Walmart CEO John Furner said in a release.

Here's how Walmart's subscription bundle compares with competitors:

Target Circle 360 is $4.99 per month or $49 per year. Amazon Prime costs $140 a year.

A standard Costco membership runs $65 a year, whereas the executive membership costs $130. For a standard BJ's membership, it's $60 per year or $120 for BJ's Club+.

The membership model is a sizeable opportunity for Walmart, per Bank of America analyst Christopher Nardone, who said in a recent note, "Walmart+ members spend approximately 4x more compared to non-members."

He added that advertising, marketplace growth, and global membership remain healthy and reaffirmed confidence "that the broader flywheel to improve longer-term profitability remains intact. "

He added, "These businesses give Walmart an advantage to navigate the challenging pricing and supply chain environment in the near term, but longer-term continued execution across these businesses should help improve longer-term profitability versus today's levels."

Deutsche Bank analyst Krisztina Katai recently upgraded the stock to a Buy rating from Neutral, citing that "the current inflationary environment should reinforce Walmart's value proposition and support accelerated share gains."

All employees will now get both memberships to Walmart and Sam's Club as part of their benefits. Last week, the company announced plans to cover over 250 medications, including insulin and inhalers for $0 and GLP-1s for diabetes.

Brooke DiPalma is a reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on X at @ BrookeDiPalma or email her at bdipalma@yahoofinance.com.

articles.title: Amazon blocks agentic AI shopping. But Walmart is betting big that it's worth saying yes.
articles.summary: Walmart's embrace of multiple AI ecosystems places the retailer in a strong position for agent-led shopping, Bank of America says.
articles.body:
Americans like to shop. For a lot of consumers, the act of browsing and filling a digital or physical cart isn't a point of friction but a way of life — just ask Costco influencers.

But in the event that more people delegate their shopping to AI agents, Walmart, and its open embrace of AI partnerships, stands to win.

That's the takeaway in a new note by Bank of America analysts led by Christopher Nardone, published Monday. They cite Walmart's integration with multiple AI ecosystems; the development of the retailer's own shopping assistant named "Sparky"; and its partnerships with other agents, including Meta's Muse, as reasons for Walmart's solid positioning.

Walmart is among the key corporate players partnering with Muse , including Best Buy ( BBY ) and Ulta ( ULTA ). These companies are attempting to embrace new modes of digital commerce.

Other retailers have taken an antagonistic approach , choosing to block Muse from interacting with their commercial portals. No doubt there are a number of reasons to block largely untested agents from inserting themselves into your business funnel. But perhaps the most obvious is to prevent another tech platform from becoming a powerful middleman.

Amazon is perhaps the most notable example. The e-commerce giant has blocked Muse from making purchases on its site and prohibits other companies from deploying automated tools to shop.

But Amazon's loss could be Walmart's gain . While Amazon may not be losing much in the way of actual sales — since most people are using AI tools to research rather than to swipe the credit card, so to speak — Walmart is trying to get in early, while habits are still forming.

Still, Walmart's management team, like everyone else, can't say for certain how popular shopping agents will become. And there are other business implications to consider if agents disrupt how people shop. As Nardone noted, if screenless computers are the ones checking out, it remains unclear what happens to the advertising landscape, a business increasingly important to Walmart itself.

Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy. Follow Hamza on X @hshaban .

articles.title: Great Scott! The AI-fueled data center build-out could double next year: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: Data centers could add about 42 times Doc Brown's 1.21 gigawatts next year, the power he needed for time travel in Back to the Future.
articles.body:
Doc Brown needed 1.21 gigawatts to send a DeLorean through time in the 1985 movie "Back to the Future." The data-center industry could add about 42 times that next year.

Research firm SemiAnalysis expects annual additions to data center IT capacity outside China to more than double next year, to about 51 gigawatts from 25 gigawatts this year.

In movie units, that's about 21 Doc Browns ballooning to 42. These are additions in a single year, not the whole fleet or the electricity it uses. By SemiAnalysis's count, that one year would roughly match the world's entire data center build-out through 2024.

About three-quarters of next year's projected additions come from projects already operational or under construction. The rest are still planned. SemiAnalysis points to more than 24 gigawatts across 40 campuses in advanced construction for expected delivery next year.

Not everyone buys it. At the All-In Summit in September, Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner called SemiAnalysis's forecast at the time, 43 gigawatts, too aggressive and guessed the industry would stand up closer to 25 gigawatts. That's only about 21 Doc Browns — no faster than this year.

How do you build that much, that quickly? Increasingly, in pieces.

Suppliers now build electrical rooms and cooling systems in factories while crews prepare the site. SemiAnalysis calls the results Lego data centers, with bricks that can weigh 50,000 pounds.

Amazon ( AMZN ) is rolling out its own modular design at large scale, and Meta Platforms ( META ) has put up tent-like halls to enclose buildings faster, according to SemiAnalysis.

A SemiAnalysis model of a 50-megawatt AI data hall puts conventional construction at 22 months and a fully modular approach at 14, excluding permitting. The biggest saving comes from electrical and mechanical installation. For the owner of the chips inside, SemiAnalysis values that eight-month head start at about $200 million.

That shift puts suppliers in the race alongside chipmakers such as Nvidia ( NVDA ). SemiAnalysis estimates content per megawatt for Vertiv ( VRT ) roughly doubles, to as much as $7 million, when it sells the full modular stack. Contractors Comfort Systems USA ( FIX ) and Sterling Infrastructure ( STRL ) assemble modules too.

But a finished building still needs power.

Microsoft ( MSFT ) confirmed Monday that it pulled out of a lease at a planned 50-megawatt Nscale data center outside London — the same size as the SemiAnalysis model — after grid officials said power might not arrive until the 2030s. Microsoft said the decision involved a single site and that its broader partnership with Nscale continues.

articles.title: Stocks are driving consumption 'like never before' — and that exposes a big risk
articles.summary: In a way that has only become true in our moment, the stock market actually is getting closer to defining the economy and consumption.
articles.body:
The stock market isn't the economy in the way that Nvidia's share price won't help your nephew find a job, or save for a down payment, or afford double meat and guac at Chipotle.

There's a level of abstraction and distance from day-to-day, working-class life that can make stock watching seem exotic. But the enormous gains of equity holdings in recent years have changed the makeup and definition of wealth in the US, with even bigger implications.

In a way that has only become true in our moment, the stock market actually is getting closer to defining the economy and consumption.

That's one of the key arguments in a note by Doug Peta, chief US investment strategist at BCA Research, published on Monday.

"The stock market isn't the economy, but it's influencing it like never before," he wrote. Peta observed that household net worth was over eight times disposable income at midyear, marking an all-time high for that measure. For decades, Wall Street has delivered outsized, compounding returns, making equities and mutual funds an ever-greater portion of household wealth.

The value of households' equity stake is nearly three times their annual after-tax income, Peta found. That means the S&P 500 gaining 10% in a year boosts a household's capacity to spend equivalent to receiving a 28% raise.

As a result, Peta wrote, stock market moves can swing consumption and overall economic activity. Combined with sharp home price appreciation, surging portfolios have augmented consumers' firepower far more than in any previous cycle, he said.

This helps explain the years-long narrative of the resilient American consumer. The people who spent their way through COVID, the aftermath, and sustained periods of high inflation. Stocks making up a higher share of a household's net worth has meant consumption is more sensitive to equity market moves. In good times, stock upswings can override other factors weighing down the economy.

"Greater sensitivity has been a boon for activity in the current cycle, as increasing equity wealth has allowed households to spend more of their paychecks than they otherwise may have," Peta wrote.

If the way the Wall Street winds are blowing has a greater say on the American consumer — because stock holdings increasingly define American wealth — that means the next bear market will have amplified influence.

Because instead of people feeling rich and spending through it, they will feel vulnerable and pull back.

In that very real sense, the stock market and the economy would sink together.

Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy. Follow Hamza on X @hshaban .

articles.title: No job, but still a 9-to-5 routine: Why China's unemployed are pretending to go to work every day
articles.summary: Tired of relatives asking, “So, where are you working now?” Some young Chinese adults have found an unusual way to dodge the question — getting dressed,
articles.body: Tired of relatives asking, “So, where are you working now?” Some young Chinese adults have found an unusual way to dodge the question — getting dressed, leaving home on time and heading out for the day.But there is one catch: they have no workplace to report to. Instead, they spend their days in libraries, parks, cafes or shopping malls, all while keeping their unemployment under wraps.Their workplace may be make-believe, but the pressure to look employed is very real.For 32-year-old Coco Li, even a photograph of lunch nearly gave away the truth. A former employee of a Chinese state-owned property firm told Reuters that she was about to post a picture of a home-cooked meal in her family group chat when she stopped herself.Sharing it could invite an obvious question from her mother: why was she at home instead of work?Li had quit her job more than six months earlier, citing a heavy workload and little recognition. But telling her family about her unemployment was not something she wanted to do. Like many others facing a difficult job market, she chose to keep up the appearance of being employed, partly to avoid the worry and pressure that would follow an admission that she was out of work."She would fall into an endless cycle of anxiety and eventually pass that anxiety on to me," Li said of her mother. Her concern, she added, "couldn't really solve my problem," she further told Reuters.Nowhere to report, everywhere to goLi's experience is part of a trend that has gained considerable attention on Chinese social media. People are sharing advice on how to fill working hours without a job, avoid questions from relatives and maintain the appearance of having somewhere to be every morning.The scale of the conversation is striking. Posts about pretend-workers and their daily routines have attracted more than 70 million views on RedNote, an Instagram-like app, and 610 million views on Douyin, China's TikTok. Related hashtags on Weibo, which is similar to X, have received up to 320 million views.Behind the online discussions lies a labour market in which securing employment has become increasingly difficult. Analysts see the trend as a reflection of the pressures facing workers in an economy increasingly dependent on strong exports.Monday's third-quarter data showed manufacturers grappling with fierce competition by cutting prices and reducing payrolls, while expecting the employees who remain to shoulder heavier workloads.The strain is not limited to manufacturing. China's prolonged property market crisis and tight local government finances have affected jobs and incomes, while automation and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence have added to employment pressures.A train to … ?For those pretending to have jobs, the challenge is not just concealing unemployment but also finding somewhere to spend the day.Social media posts describe people moving between parks, libraries, cafes and shopping malls, keeping themselves occupied until it is time to return home. The routines recall those of salarymen in South Korea and Japan who concealed their joblessness during the Asian financial crisis of the 1990s.Li follows a similar routine when her parents come to visit.The crowds in places that might otherwise seem quiet on a weekday have also caught the attention of people experiencing the same predicament. Zhang, a 36-year-old visual effects producer who lost her job in AI-driven redundancies in August, gave only her surname."I never would have believed the library would be completely full on a weekday," she said.Online, the stories range from practical guides to personal accounts of unemployment. Some users wonder whether strangers around them are also pretending to be at work. Others explain why they have chosen to hide their circumstances and describe the emotional toll of keeping up the act.One post, titled "Day 30 of unemployment: a month pretending to work," documents a month of joblessness alongside 80 unsuccessful job applications.And the pretence gets harderFor Susan Sun, 28, keeping her unemployment private has become a daily exercise in managing time and appearances.Sun has concealed her layoff from an internet company since late last year. The arrangement became more difficult in May, when her mother and stepfather moved from their smaller hometown to live with her in the megacity of Chongqing as they looked for work.With her parents at home, Sun has to leave before 9 am and return after 6 pm, maintaining the rhythm of a working day even though she no longer has a job.She gets by on monthly unemployment benefits of 1,864 yuan ($278) and the remaining money from her severance package. Sun says she is content to live on little and not work. The pressure comes instead from her parents and their concerns about her finances."They pass their anxiety on to me, through subtle, insistent expressions and tone of voice," she said.The concern becomes particularly apparent when they urge her to save money because "the economy is bad."For Sun, therefore, the difficulty is not simply finding a way to occupy her time. It is also avoiding conversations that turn her financial circumstances into a source of anxiety within the family.Keeping up appearances to keep the peaceThe decision to hide unemployment can have consequences beyond individual households. Diana Fu, an associate professor of Chinese politics at Cornell University, said pretending to go to work gives people a way to save face and could also help defuse collective discontent.She said the practice helps preserve social stability as Beijing presses ahead with automation and its technological competition with the US."Pretend-workers are helping the Chinese government to stave off the hard choice between leaping ahead in automation and protecting job security, which is so essential to the social contract," she said.For those involved, however, the arrangement is also a way of managing the expectations of family members at a time when work is becoming harder to find.The pretence may offer temporary relief from difficult questions, but maintaining it requires time, effort and money — resources that can become increasingly scarce during unemployment.Financial pressure could eventually make it harder for unemployed people to continue concealing their circumstances. Yige Dong, an assistant professor of sociology at the University at Buffalo, said that China's social safety net is relatively thin compared with the support systems available in Japan and South Korea during the 1990s.You use AI every day. articles.title: GM beats on Q3 results, tightens profit outlook, and unveils new $20 billion buyback
articles.summary: GM posted third quarter results before the bell that topped estimates.
articles.body:
GM ( GM ) posted third quarter results before the bell that topped estimates, tightened its full-year profit outlook instead of boosting it, but issued shareholders a new $20 billion share repurchase program instead.

For the quarter, GM posted Q3 revenue of $50.0 billion, up 2.9% from a year ago and above the $48.52 billion Bloomberg consensus. GM posted adjusted EPS of $3.70 vs $3.57 estimated, with adjusted EBIT coming in at $4.1 billion, ahead of the $4.02 billion expected and up nearly 22%.

But the big update was guidance. For the full year, GM now expects:

Adjusted EBIT of $14.5 billion-$15.5 billion (prior $14.0 billion-$16.0 billion)

Adjusted EPS of $12.75-$13.75 (prior $12.00-$14.00)

Adjusted automotive free cash flow of $11.5 billion-$12.5 billion (prior $9.5 billion-$11.5 billion)

Both ranges keep the same midpoints as before — $15 billion and $13.25 — meaning GM trimmed the upside as much as the downside.

The real raise came on cash. GM lifted its adjusted automotive free cash flow forecast to $11.5 billion-$12.5 billion, from $9.5 billion-$11.5 billion.

GM's board approved a new $20 billion multiyear authorization with no expiration date. GM also declared a quarterly dividend of $0.18 per share.

"We think this is a proven strategy," GM CEO Mary Barra wrote in her letter to shareholders. "The new $20 billion multiyear share repurchase authorization we announced today further demonstrates our board's commitment to creating even greater shareholder value."

Barra also said GM is working to continue its momentum "despite growing inflationary pressures."

This is seen with GM's costs creeping up. GM now expects commodity inflation of about $2 billion (the top of its prior $1.5 billion-$2 billion range), including logistics and memory chip (DRAM) costs. It also cut its expected regulatory benefits to about $500 million from as much as $750 million. Offsetting that, gross tariff costs are tracking toward the low end of its $2.5 billion-$3.5 billion range.

Earlier this month, GM reported third quarter US sales of 670,974 vehicles , a drop of 5.5% compared to a year ago, as a collapse in EV sales offset gains from its pickups and small SUV s.

Based on GM's model-by-model figures, EV sales fell about 62% to roughly 25.5K units, shrinking to under 4% of GM's US volume from more than 9% a year ago. Excluding EVs, GM's sales were essentially flat, up 0.3%.

Sales of the Chevrolet Equinox EV plunged 92.4% to 1,905, the Blazer EV dropped 84.4%, the GMC Hummer EV slid 72.9%, and the Cadillac Lyriq fell 50.5%.

articles.title: Cook working in a 5-star hotel gets Rs 4 crore tax notice with penalty for alleged Rs 24.62 crore sales, but he claims PAN was misused which led to wrong Form 26AS entry; why Delhi HC gave relief
articles.summary: What happens if your PAN Card is misused and the entry shows up in your Form 26AS, prompting an income tax notice and tax demand way above your salary?
articles.body: What happens if your PAN Card is misused and the entry shows up in your Form 26AS, prompting an income tax notice and tax demand way above your salary?In one such case a man received a tax notice along with a penalty claim for purported cash sales worth Rs 24.62 crore. Incidentally, the man earned a salary that was not even taxable. Here’s how the case unfolded:What the case is aboutIn 2024, a cook employed at a 5-star hotel in Delhi received an income tax notice demanding nearly Rs 4 crore in tax, along with a penalty for under-reporting income.The notice alleged that the man had made cash sales worth Rs 24.62 crore through a company dealing in packing materials.He immediately checked his Form 26AS to understand why such a large transaction was linked to his tax records.Also Read | Husband and wife sell property; Income Tax dept alleges Rs 3.30 crore sale against Rs 1.60 crore in deed, cites WhatsApp chats, Excel sheets to claim Rs 1.70 crore cash receipts, but ITAT gives reliefThe document showed an entry against his Permanent Account Number (PAN) for cash sales of Rs 24.62 crore. The form also indicated that tax had been deducted at source (TDS) at 1% on the reported amount.He suspected that his PAN details had been misused, so the man approached the Greater Kailash Police Station in New Delhi and the Delhi Police Cyber Cell in Saket to lodge formal complaints.The Income Tax Department's Assessing Officer (AO) did not accept his explanation. The man was told that the tax law required him either to pay the outstanding demand or challenge the order before the appropriate authority.Challenging the demand, however, was not easy. With the tax liability standing at nearly Rs 4 crore, the man would have had to deposit around Rs 78 lakh in advance. He therefore approached the Delhi High Court.The man told the court that he had no taxable income and had never carried out the transaction referred to in the tax notice. He maintained that his PAN details had been used by someone else without his knowledge.His advocate argued that the man was a victim of identity theft and that an unidentified person had misused his PAN credentials. He pointed out that the man had no connection with the packing materials company mentioned in the notice, as his occupation was that of a cook.The advocate further submitted that the man had been working as a contractual employee. During his employment, he had worked for several contractors and provided them with copies of his PAN card for verification. According to the advocate, one of these copies could have been misused, resulting in the disputed transaction being linked to the man’s tax records.Also Read | US-based homebuyer paid Rs 15 lakh for Rs 10.41 lakh flat, but builder demanded Rs 20 lakh more and allegedly threatened him; commission orders refund with 12% interest and Rs 10 lakh compensationThe lawyer also contended that the mere appearance of the Permanent Account Number in Tax Collected at Source records, Form 26AS or the annual tax summary was not sufficient grounds to impose a tax demand. Without additional evidence connecting the man to the transaction, the reported amount could not automatically be treated as his business turnover or receipts.On October 6, 2026, the Delhi High Court ruled in the man’s favour, providing him relief by cancelling the entire tax demand notice.Why did the man win the case?Pranshu G, Partner at Ashok Pranshu & Co, told ET that the Delhi High Court found that the assessment against the man relied entirely on Form 26AS and information available on the tax portal. There was no independent evidence establishing that he had carried out the transactions in question.The man’s employment background, bank statements and financial circumstances supported his contention that his PAN had been misused.Despite this, the assessing officer disregarded his explanation and the police complaints he had filed. The officer also failed to provide the underlying evidence or conduct an inquiry with the company allegedly involved in the transactions, according to the ET report quoting the judgement.Also Read | She bought shares for Rs 13.5 lakh and sold them for Rs 77.47 lakh after 18 months; taxman denied capital gains exemption, but ITAT gives relief and deletes Rs 79 lakh in additionsDuring the hearing, the Delhi High Court questioned the Income Tax Department about the evidence it had gathered beyond the man’s Form 26AS. The court also sought to know whether the department had carried out an independent investigation or recorded the statement of the owner of the packaging company to establish that the alleged transactions had actually taken place with the man.The Delhi High Court also pointed out that the AO could have issued a notice under Section 133(6) of the Income-tax Act to the packaging company, seeking further information or recording its statement to establish whether the transactions had taken place.Another error identified in the assessment was the double counting of the gross and net amounts relating to the same transaction by the tax officer.In the response reproduced in the assessment order, the man had explained that he withdrew money from his provident fund (PF) account between 2013 and 2018 to meet his financial requirements. He had also obtained an Economically Weaker Section (EWS) certificate and applied for a waiver of school fees for his children.The court said these circumstances called for an empathetic approach, careful scrutiny and a detailed examination of the facts rather than a mechanical assessment of the available information.The Delhi High Court said: “Because, these facts clearly suggested that petitioner’s defence that someone had misused his PAN number, had some substance.”Emphasising the need for tax authorities to balance enforcement with a realistic assessment of the facts, the Delhi High Court said: “A Tax Enforcement Officer should strive to achieve high revenue target but he should keep his feet firmly grounded on the floor of reality. His eyes should be sharp to pierce through the fraud but they should not slip away from the facts.”Also Read | He bought a home, gave it for redevelopment years later and sold new flat for Rs 1.95 crore within 8 days; taxman denied LTCG exemption and added Rs 80.14 lakh, but ITAT grants reliefPranshu said these lapses amounted to a violation of the principles of natural justice and constitutional safeguards against arbitrary action.Pranshu said: "Given the man’s limited means, the appellate remedy was considered ineffective. Fresh proceedings remain permissible only upon other cogent evidence linking him to the transactions, within statutory limitation."The court ultimately granted the man complete relief and quashed the tax demand notice. However, it clarified that the Income Tax Department could reopen the case in the future if it discovered incriminating evidence linking him to the alleged transactions.You use AI every day. articles.title: France’s growing debt woes: How bond markets set countries’ borrowing costs
articles.summary: France’s rising debt is unnerving investors, but countries such as the US and Japan owe even greater sums.
articles.body:
France’s borrowing costs have surged amid the worst social unrest in the country in decades.

Yields on French bonds have risen to their highest levels in nearly a quarter of a century as investors demand higher returns for taking on government debt. The surge reflects a growing conviction in bond markets that lending to France is becoming an increasingly risky proposition.

While France is grappling with a widening gap between government spending and revenues, the country’s fragmented political landscape is bitterly divided on how to plug the hole.

Meanwhile, hundreds of thousands of protesters, some of whom have participated in rioting and looting, have taken to the streets to oppose proposed budget cuts and demand greater spending on cost-of-living relief and public services such as education.

France’s national debt is now at its highest level since the immediate aftermath of World War II, nearing 120 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

How do bonds work and why are France’s borrowing costs rising?

Bonds are a type of loan to a government or corporation. Countries routinely borrow from bond markets to allow spending that is not covered by tax revenues.

In exchange for buying a bond, an investor is paid regular interest payments, plus the original borrowed sum at a set date in the future. These bonds can be traded on the bond market to other investors in the meantime.

Bond prices are influenced by interest rates, inflation and confidence in the issuer’s ability to repay the loan, among other factors.

When bond prices rise, bond yields fall, and vice versa.

France’s 10-year bond yield has risen more than 130 basis points since June, topping 4.9 percent.

France’s borrowing costs now stand at their highest levels since 2002, swallowing up a growing share of tax revenues that could otherwise be directed towards essential services such as education and healthcare.

While France’s debt levels are relatively high, the amount that a country owes is just one consideration for investors pricing the risk of its bonds.

Market confidence in a country’s ability to meet its obligations is shaped by a range of factors, including the economy’s strength, the amount of its external debt versus domestic debt and the ability of the political system to govern effectively.

“The sustainability of sovereign debt is rarely determined by its absolute level alone,” Victor Lequillerier, president of BSI Economics, a think tank in Paris, told Al Jazeera.

“It depends far more on its trajectory, structure, and broader economic and financial context.”

In France’s case, the paralysis of the country’s political system is a key driver of concern in the bond markets currently.

In the fragmented National Assembly, French Prime Minister Ssbastien Lecornu, who was appointed by President Emmanuel Macron under the country’s semi-presidential system, is mired in a legislative battle to pass a budget for next year that includes 54 billion euros ($61bn) in savings.

Marine Le Pen of far-right National Rally and Jean-Luc Melenchon of far-left France Unbowed, the two leading candidates in next year’s presidential election, are opposed to Lecornu’s proposals, though the government could invoke a constitutional clause to bypass parliament if deemed necessary.

Antonio Fatas, a professor of economics at INSEAD in Fontainebleau, France, told Al Jazeera: “Are the French numbers much worse than other countries? No, but marginally they are worse, and the real difficulty here is that the political situation is such that the current government does not have an easy path to put together a budget that makes sense from a debt sustainability point of view.”

He added: “That’s what makes France a special case now, that’s why markets are very much worried about what France is going through and why you see a lot of the noise.”

France’s national debt, at about 3.6 trillion euros ($4 trillion), is equivalent to 119 percent of GDP, up from 98 percent in 2019, the year before the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Of greater concern to markets than the total debt is France’s ballooning deficit, however, which is expected to reach 5.4 percent of GDP in 2026 – far above the European Union average of just more than 3 percent. This is the amount by which a government’s spending exceeds its income.

France, which has a strong tradition of left-wing politics and activism, has long had one of the biggest public sectors in the developed world.

Government spending is equivalent to about 57 percent of GDP, second only to Finland among Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries.

Public pensions make up a particularly large proportion of expenditure, amounting to 14 percent of GDP, a figure that is likely to rise as the country’s working-age population shrinks in the coming decades.

“Ironically, President Macron has long discussed the reforms needed to improve the fiscal outlook and avoid attracting the ire of bond investors,” Alex Dryden, a macroeconomist at the Centre for Sustainable Finance at SOAS University of London, told Al Jazeera.

“From 2017 onwards, Macron has spoken of the need for pension reforms to ease the fiscal burden, but this is a lightning-rod political issue in France and attempts at reforms have stalled on multiple occasions.”

“Tackling this issue would resolve much of France’s fiscal burden, but that is much easier said than done,” Dryden added.

While France levies some of the highest taxes of any country to support its sizeable welfare state, its budget deficit widened substantially during the pandemic and has remained above the recent historical trend ever since.

Exacerbating the shortfall has been a long-running trend of anaemic growth, which saw the French economy expand by just 59 percent of the OECD average from 2000 to 2025.

GDP is forecast to grow just 0.4 percent this year, following a 0.9 percent expansion in 2025.

BSI Economics’ Lequillerier said the French government has spent years shirking the kind of budgetary reforms that reduced the deficits of heavily indebted peers such as Italy, Spain and Portugal.

“In the post-pandemic period, most European economies managed to normalise their fiscal positions and bring deficits closer to sustainable levels. France, however, failed to do so, with public spending growth persistently overwhelming revenue dynamics,” Lequillerier said.

Lequillerier said investors’ tolerance for the government’s lack of fiscal restraint has finally run out.

“The correction is becoming increasingly painful, and France risks isolating itself within the euro area as its principal fiscal underperformer,” he said.

Why is France under more pressure than countries with higher levels of debt?

While relatively high, France’s debt is lower than that of several other economies, including the United States, Japan and Italy.

But in each of those cases, there are specific circumstances that mitigate the risks.

The US is better positioned than its peers to manage massive debt levels due to the status of the US dollar as the world’s primary reserve currency, which allows it to borrow money relatively cheaply and in greater amounts.

Japan has been able to sustain a debt-to-GDP ratio of more than 200 percent because most of its debt is held by domestic institutions, insulating it from capital flight. Monetary authorities have also kept interest rates at ultralow levels.

Italy’s debt-to-GDP ratio of 140 percent is higher than that of France, but it also has a smaller budget deficit equivalent to about 3 percent of GDP.

“The total debt burden that a government can support depends on quite a few things and varies between countries,” Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics, told Al Jazeera.

“For example, investors will get more anxious if the country’s economy is only slowly growing, or not at all, and if the government deficit is very high, which – all else equal – means the debt ratio will tend to rise. And the debt burden a country can support also depends on who wants to buy that country’s debt,” Kenningham said.

France is also under pressure, in part, because there are more options in the bond market for investors to look at than in the past, said Lequillerier at BSI Economics.

“Germany is now running larger deficits and issuing substantially more debt, while Italy and Spain have strengthened both their fiscal positions,” he said.

“France therefore faces much stiffer competition for international capital within the euro-denominated sovereign bond market.”

While France’s finances are far from unsalvageable, the longer the government takes to tighten its belt, the greater the risks of a full-blown debt crisis, economists say.

“What is the likelihood of France going into a debt crisis? Enough that it should worry us,” INSEAD’s Fatas said. “As an economist, I could say the numbers are not too bad.”

“We can find a budget that would put France in a more sustainable position, but that requires certain compromises, and that requires certain political choices, very, very difficult to do in the current environment,” he said.

Lequillerier of BSI Economics said while a French default is not a realistic possibility, the country would suffer a “profound loss of economic credibility” if it had to seek assistance from an institution like the European Central Bank or the IMF.

“This is not the central scenario today,” he said. “Nevertheless, the longer fiscal adjustment is delayed, the less remote such an outcome becomes.”

articles.title: Why can’t I afford life? Boomer prosperity is masking a weak economy.
articles.summary: So which party has a better plan for addressing this problem and getting you a fair shot at the American Dream? The bad news is, the answer is “neither.”
articles.body:
We have only two weeks until the midterm elections, when American voters will decide whether to give President Trump’s party or his Democratic opponents control of the House and the Senate.

For most Americans, this election is about the cost of living, and it’s no wonder why: Inflation rose by 0.6 percent in September and is up 3.7 percent this year. Half of that is due to the rise in energy costs. Wholesale inflation surged by 1.3 percent and is now at its highest level since December 2022.

The number of homes sold this year has plummeted to its lowest level since 2014, and that is no surprise either. Who can afford to buy a house in this economy?

Although Trump keeps insisting that this is the “Golden Age of America,” millions feel absolutely strapped due to the exploding cost of living, with which wages have simply not kept up in many key categories. Home prices are up nearly 60 percent. Rent is up 33 percent. Groceries are up 32 percent. Electricity is up 46 percent. Gas is up 69 percent. Health care is up 20 percent.

These just aren’t budget items you can opt out of. In other words, Americans don’t just feel broke — they are broke.

But not all Americans are broke. New data out of the Federal Reserve found that between 2022 and 2025, the real net worth of the average American family rose by only 2 percent. But for the richest and oldest Americans their net worth skyrocketed by more than 30 percent. Wealth increased by 37 percent for Americans 75 and older, while it declined 23 percent for people under 35.

Just think about that: Young Americans just getting started in life saw a 23 percent decrease in their net worth, whereas the oldest Americans — the most well off, the most secure, those having retired after spending a lifetime building wealth — saw their own net worth increase by nearly 40 percent.

The median net worth of the oldest households in America jumped from around $366,000 to just over $500,000 over the last three years, whereas for Americans under 35, it fell from $42,000 to $32,000. And in the course of losing nearly a quarter of their wealth, younger millennials have to struggle to pay off twice as much debt as Boomers.

In short, your parents are millionaires, and you can’t afford rent.

Americans 55 and over are now worth $140 trillion — roughly three-quarters of the nation’s net worth — even though they represent less than one-third of all Americans, according to a Bank of America Institute analysis . Of course, not all older Americans are so fortunate. One-third of Boomers have no retirement savings. The wealthiest 10 percent control 71 percent of Boomer wealth.

Their prosperity is concealing a much weaker economy overall. The top 10 percent of spenders now account for more than half of all consumer spending.

And Boomers have been famously reluctant to move out of their homes, resulting in a massive housing crunch that has been keeping millennials out of homeownership and driving up the cost of homes by 55 percent since 2020. Empty-nest Boomers are now sitting on almost 30 percent of homes with three or more bedrooms — nearly twice the rate of Millennials with kids.

And the oldsters are about to get even more help with a cost of living adjustment to their Social Security benefits, which are set to increase by 3.6 percent in 2027, boosting the average retiree’s annual benefits by $900.

Our economy has become an upward funnel of wealth from struggling young people to secure and prosperous old people. The most strapped generation is paying for the benefits of the least strapped, with no guarantee they will get similar benefits in their old age. Social Security, which young people are now paying for, will likely be bankrupt by the time they need it.

Young families just starting out are also buckling under crushing medical bills while paying for the Medicare used by older and much richer Americans.

This intolerable state of affairs explains why so many young people have given up on capitalism altogether and want to give socialism a chance.

So which party has a better plan for addressing this problem and getting you a fair shot at the American Dream? The bad news is, the answer is “neither.”

The Democrats’ big plan to get down the cost of energy is to ban fossil fuels. Their big plan to make health care affordable is to make you pay even more for overpriced and suboptimal ObamaCare-subsidized health plans that you don’t even use. Their big plan to get down the cost of groceries is non-existent.

But it’s not clear that Republicans party have much of a plan for these things, either. Trump is not campaigning like he has a plan to address these problems, or like he even understands them. He spends his rallies touting the Golden Age of America, calling us the “hottest country around” and declaring the affordability crisis a “hoax.”

Taking seriously the injustice of an economy that forces those with the least to subsidize the lives of those with the most is absolutely essential for any politician hoping to succeed in 2026, 2028, and beyond.

Batya Ungar Sargon is the host of “ Batya !” which airs Saturday nights at 7 p.m. Eastern Time on NewsNation, the nation’s fastest-growing cable news network and a sister company of The Hill.

articles.title: Canary in the coal mine or just a bad apple? CoreWeave debt drama roils Wall Street
articles.summary: Wall Street is increasingly scrutinizing the massive debt companies are taking on to fund the artificial intelligence boom.
articles.body: Wall Street is increasingly scrutinizing the massive debt companies are taking on to fund the artificial intelligence boom. Rising interest rates and uncertainty about the pace of the data center buildout are fueling concerns about whether heavily indebted AI companies will be able to earn enough to pay it all back. CoreWeave (CRWV) is at the center of the turmoil. The New Jersey-based tech company is part of a niche sub-industry called neoclouds that rent computing power to companies building AI technology. It’s a high-growth opportunity for investors, given expectations for intense AI demand. But CoreWeave is relying on debt to fund its growth. The company has come under pressure this month as its bond yields surged to levels that signal distress. Rising interest rates are putting pressure on the company, which isn’t profitable. The company’s shares have dropped 30% this month. And it’s making Wall Street wonder: Is CoreWeave a canary in the coal mine, or a case of a bad apple in an otherwise healthy orchard? Investors are trying to discern whether CoreWeave’s troubles could create systemic problems for the AI boom. “Canary in the coal mine implies that if CoreWeave fails, that the whole ecosystem is going to fall, that the whole AI economy is going to fail. I don’t think that’s the case,” Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, told CNN. “The AI economy is full of good behavior and bad behavior,” Luria said. “They are a bad apple, but there’s other bad apples. They just represent some of this bad behavior.” In a fresh sign of doubts about whether the billions flowing to AI companies can be justified, AI data center company Elice Group plunged 32% on its trading debut in South Korea Tuesday. The IPO flop will only add to concerns about valuations and returns across the sector. AI debt in focus CoreWeave had roughly $52 billion in debt and lease liabilities on its balance sheet in the second quarter. That’s up from roughly $30 billion at the end of 2025. Meanwhile, the cost of borrowing has climbed as bond yields have surged this year. Smaller, debt-laden companies are more vulnerable and exposed to the pain of higher interest rates. As of last week, the interest on some of CoreWeave’s bonds surged to 15% — a level that signals distress or a higher risk of default. Investors are more concerned that CoreWeave won’t earn enough returns to pay back all the money it borrowed. CoreWeave exemplifies the risk of “funding speculative investments with debt,” Luria said. Since CoreWeave went public in 2025, Luria said he’s been skeptical about the amount of debt the company is taking on without a clear path to profitability. With enormous amounts of debt on its balance sheet, the company is vulnerable to sharp moves in interest rates, as well as any signs of a slowdown in the data center buildout. As public backlash to data centers mounts, investors are trying to discern whether moratoriums or other hurdles could hamper forecasts for size and completion of data center projects. We’ve been here before… sort of Uncertainty about the health of CoreWeave contributed to a slide in tech stocks last week. But Wall Street analysts argue the reaction might be overdone. Markets have seen this kind of reaction from investors before when rising interest rates start to spark turmoil — and it wasn’t always rational or warranted. In 2023, a series of regional bank failures sparked concerns that rising interest rates were ushering in a widespread crisis. “It was a plausible argument. It was also wrong,” Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chairman of research at Barclays, wrote in a Monday note. “Similarly, investors shouldn’t extrapolate recent challenges for CoreWeave debt to a view on the entire AI capex cycle,” he wrote. What’s next for CoreWeave and AI? CoreWeave’s enormous debt load is concerning for the value of the stock, but there isn’t a systemic risk for the AI buildout, analysts say. Ultimately, the demand for AI is real and will continue to power the boom. “The only systemic risk to the ecosystem right now, is if people stop using AI and aren’t willing to pay for it,” Luria said. “I actually think that demand for AI is growing so fast that any potential failures are probably down the road.” Wall Street is still feeling confident about the Big Tech companies powering the AI boom like Alphabet, Microsoft and Nvidia. These are some of the largest publicly traded companies in the world. As long as demand for computing power exceeds the supply, these Big Tech titans will have the incentive to keep building. Higher interest rates are a pain, but not enough to dissuade them from building. Still, the Big Tech titans have been burning through cash as they spend more money on the AI buildout. Wall Street analysts are trying to discern whether Big Tech will continue to burn cash or not. If more debt is used, higher rates could become more of a problem. “Our downfall is always when we take on too much debt,” Luria said. “It’s unnecessary, but times of boom and opportunity and frontier end up becoming a form of the Wild West, and bad behavior ensues.” “That doesn’t mean the growth is wrong or the technology is bad,” Luria said. “It just means that there’s bad behavior that usually follows large growth cycles.”
