articles.title: Oil parked above $110 a barrel as IEA warns energy markets won’t return to normal next year
articles.summary: Global energy markets are more than a year away from returning to normal and remain highly vulnerable to “overlapping crises” in the Middle East, the head of the International Energy Agency has warned.
articles.body: Global energy markets are more than a year away from returning to normal and remain highly vulnerable to “overlapping crises” in the Middle East, the head of the International Energy Agency has warned. His comments come as oil prices have been marching upwards in recent weeks. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, is trading above $111 a barrel. If it stays there, it could settle at its highest level since May. “I don’t see any credible pathway that 2027 will be a year of normalisation,” IEA executive director Fatih Birol told an industry gathering in London Tuesday. The Strait of Hormuz has been closed once, “it can be closed again,” he said. The waterway, which transported a fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas supply before the war, has become heavily contested with attacks on ships ramping up in recent weeks. “I’m very worried that there will be some overlapping crises in the Middle East … and it may further escalate the situation, which will have serious implications for energy markets,” Birol told the Financial Times Energy Transition Summit. Higher oil prices reflect concerns that the US-Iran conflict could escalate. Iran has signalled that it is preparing for another round of war, issuing public threats against Washington in an apparent bid to deter President Donald Trump from reigniting the current stalemated conflict. At the same time, Saudi Arabia has faced deadly attacks from Iran-backed Houthi militants in recent weeks, disrupting oil shipments and prompting the kingdom to call off its flagship investor conference, planned for later this month, just a week before it was due to take place. “I have many, many concerns about the situation,” Birol said at the Financial Times Energy Transition Summit. He cautioned that assessing the depth of the current energy crisis by looking only at crude prices – which have not gone as high as $200 a barrel, as some analysts had predicted at the start of the war – was “myopic.” “We don’t use crude oil, we use products,” he noted, pointing to the fact that diesel prices have doubled from levels before the war, due largely to the Iran war but also in part to attacks on refineries in Russia. “We are entering a season where diesel demand typically goes up” and many large refineries have planned maintenance work, he said. “We are on thin ice and I am very worried about this.” He said that IEA member countries, which total 32, “will not hesitate to look into the option of releasing further stocks” of oil reserves should they be needed. IEA members agreed a historic release of emergency reserves in March, with 80% of those 400 million barrels already issued to the market and 20% still to be released. Member countries still have about 1.6 billion barrels “in pocket,” noted Birol. “We are keeping it for the rainy days.”

articles.title: Trump announces $8 billion for farmers to offset soaring diesel costs
articles.summary: President Trump just announced aid for farmers to pay for soaring diesel costs.
articles.body:
President Trump announced an $8 billion aid package on Monday to help US farmers pay for diesel this harvest season.

The relief program, announced at a campaign rally in Kansas and on social media, aims to bring down fuel costs for Americans ahead of next month's midterm elections.

"Tonight, I am also pleased to announce that the Department of Agriculture will be launching a new 'Harvest Fuel Relief Program,' providing our Farmers with 8 BILLION DOLLARS in support to offset Diesel costs during this Harvest Season," Trump's account posted on Truth Social ( DJT ).

"When Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our Great Farmers, and Fuel prices will come tumbling down as soon as the Iran War is over, which will happen very quickly!" he added.

The Harvest Fuel Relief Program will be administered by the US Department of Agriculture. Trump credited Republican Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas with helping advance the initiative.

The White House move comes as nearly every corner of the economy, including farming and transportation, grapples with soaring energy input costs.

Diesel prices on Monday hovered near a national average of $6.31 per gallon after hitting a record high in September, driven by conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as constrained global refining capacity.

The aid program won't directly lower fuel costs but is expected to provide one-time payments, administered by the Farm Service Agency (FSA), to help farmers offset these expenses.

Earlier this month, the Trump administration moved to lift restrictions on red-dyed diesel, a tax-exempt fuel typically reserved for tractors and farm gear. The measure allows its use in standard highway vehicles.

Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.
